# We Documented 1,200+ Actions by ICE. Here's What We Found.


A new ACLU report reveals the scale of civil rights violations committed by ICE and the police forces it has deputized — from racial profiling to school lockdowns.


[Naureen Shah](https://www.aclu.org/bios/naureen-shah) ,
ACLU National Political Advocacy Division


**Share This Page**


July 16, 2026


Just last week, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) shot and killed a man in Houston, Texas who had lived in the country for 35 years; he was a father to three sons and a business owner. ICE didn’t even allege that he posed a danger at the time, or had committed crimes in the past. This wasn’t a lone occurrence: Senior White House official Tom Homan recently admitted that at least[half of those ICE is currently arresting have no criminal record](https://x.com/EricLDaugh/status/2074278314496188823?s=20) . And days later, ICE shot another man in Maine.


A new ACLU report, “[Agents of Chaos and Cruelty](https://www.aclu.org/publications/agents-of-chaos-and-cruelty-how-the-trump-administrations-national-deportation-policing-force-has-attacked-american-communities) ,” illustrates how these types of headline-making abuses committed by ICE are the tip of an iceberg. We closely reviewed and documented more than 1,200 incidents that occurred in eight states in 2025. We found that ICE and the agents working for them — together, what we call the national deportation policing force — have adopted methods and routine tactics that frequently lead to serious civil rights violations. They are committing these violations at a scale and severity without precedent in our nation’s recent history.


The Trump administration is ramping up immigration arrests and deportations to[record-breaking](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/01/us/politics/ice-immigrant-arrests-surge.html) levels. Instead of surging into one city at a time — as we saw in Minneapolis and Los Angeles, for instance — the administration is escalating its deportation efforts in communities across the country, at the same time. A larger-than-ever ICE, together with the thousands of state and local police they have deputized, is attempting to arrest scores of people on American streets in the coming weeks to meet a quota. These street arrests, which ICE has never previously conducted at this scale, will endanger everyone’s rights and safety.


## Turning American Streets Into Deportation Zones


**The Trump administration has repeatedly characterized its actions as targeting “the worst of the worst,” but the reality is that no one is safe from its indiscriminate deportation drive. We identified numerous people who were detained, targeted, or subjected to law enforcement misconduct by the national deportation policing force, including:**


- 782 protestors, journalists, elected officials, clergy, and community observers
- 214 children, including 32 who were U.S. citizens
- 155 U.S. citizens


**The Trump administration has turned American streets into deportation zones, changing the nature of American life. In our research, we also identified:**


- 624 instances when everyday locations like grocery stores, bus stops, and gas stations became the sites of immigration arrests
- 437 likely instances of racial profiling, which has become rampant
- 49 times the national deportation policing force was deployed at or near schools, prompting 40 school lockdowns
- 418 times agents pushed, shoved, tackled, or pinned people and 81 instances when agents used tactics that can limit breathing and become deadly, such as chokeholds
- 361 instances when agents deployed chemical irritants, including 132 times directly aimed at individuals


**Agents made the threat of deadly force part of ordinary enforcement – and the cases we reviewed reveal the recklessness of agents. Examples include:**


- In Hyattsville, Maryland, agents pinned a man in a busy intersection, pressing against his neck, when one dropped his gun. After scrambling to retrieve it, he turned it toward the crowd. A second agent later drew his weapon and moved toward bystanders.
- In Simi Valley, California, agents detained Rodrigo Almendarez, a U.S. citizen born in Canoga Park, outside his job at a roofing and building supply company. Agents left their SUV in drive when they grabbed him; the SUV rolled forward while one agent chased after it, striking a tree and shattering a side mirror.
- In Bowie, Maryland, agents arrested a father after he had just left home to drive his children to school in the family minivan. His three children — ages 6, 7, and 8 — were in the backseat as masked agents smashed his window, pulled him from the car, pinned him to the ground, pressed a hand on his neck, and pointed a Taser at him while he was pinned. The children later told their mother they saw agents point a gun at their father; video shows an agent pointing the Taser. He was detained one day after his wife said he had checked in for immigration supervision.


This civil rights data is among the largest that has ever been reported regarding ICE, and is based on our meticulous research and analysis. It’s not a full accounting of ICE’s street enforcement actions in 2025 — which exploded to unprecedented levels — but it is a striking sample. The data also expose the gaps in our accountability structures, which largely failed to stop agents who routinely threatened public safety in communities across the country.


## The Blueprint for Authoritarian Rule


The tactics that “Agents of Chaos and Cruelty *”* details are straight from the authoritarian playbook. The Trump administration deploys anti-immigrant scapegoating and nearly explicit white supremacist narratives, even featuring white supremacist slogans and images in its recruitment campaigns. Its deportation drive also involves suppressing dissent, evading checks and balances, and consolidating executive power.


In 2025, senior officials created a national deportation policing force of officers who often appeared masked and menacing in our communities. They treated it as the president’s personal force to be deployed against American cities perceived as hostile to his interests, during political standoffs with the opposing party, and in response to protests. Now, the national deportation policing force is — with little public notice — operating all over the country, with state and local police conducting traffic stops and setting up checkpoints for immigration enforcement.


What we are experiencing mirrors aspects of countries under authoritarian rule, where the loss of basic freedoms grows so widespread that it seems less remarkable over time and simply becomes a fact of life. We must prevent the abuses we’ve seen across the country from becoming an accepted, new normal.


## Transforming Our System: The ACLU’s Affirmative Vision


It is time for transformative change to an immigration system that has long been cruel and dysfunctional, and has proven vulnerable to exploitation for authoritarian ends. Nearly 25 years since the creation of the Department of Homeland Security and its component agency ICE, our immigration system requires a hard reset.


“Agents of Chaos and Cruelty” is the first in a new series of ACLU papers and reports making the case for the new immigration system we envision. This system would replace ICE’s abuses with “a new cabinet-level Immigration Management Agency oriented toward service — with a mission to keep families together, support American communities and meet the needs of the American workforce.” Our democracy needs an immigration system built with safe, fair, and proportionate tools to hold people accountable to our immigration laws — not a vast paramilitary force operating with claimed immunity and punishing people with deadly, unjust, and unnecessary mass civil detention.


Congress must finally enact a path to citizenship so that millions of our loved ones and neighbors can gain lasting and real protection from deportation, and the equal rights and all protections under the law afforded by citizenship. Bills like the American Dream and Promise Act, which would extend a path to citizenship to an estimated 4.4 million Americans-in-waiting, should be at the top of Congress’ agenda. Congress must also dismantle the national deportation policing force, including by ending ICE’s misuse of state and local police through the 287(g) program. It should rescind the $240 billion in no-strings-attached funding it has provided to our immigration agencies; that money should go to supporting our communities, not attacking them.


Achieving transformative change to our immigration system will require all of us to call our members of Congress, state legislators, and city councils, and keep sharing why this matters.


[Read the full report.](https://www.aclu.org/publications/agents-of-chaos-and-cruelty-how-the-trump-administrations-national-deportation-policing-force-has-attacked-american-communities)

### Immigrants’ Rights Organizations File Lawsuit to Stop ICE from Hiding Locations of Detained People


BOSTON — A group of legal services organizations today filed a lawsuit challenging the federal government’s new policy of hiding the locations of thousands of people detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The policy unlawfully interferes with communication between detainees, their families, and their lawyers. The lawsuit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts on behalf of Greater Boston Legal Services, Rian Immigrant Center, Florence Immigrant and Refugee Rights Project, and Amica Center for Immigrant Rights. The groups argue the new policy unlawfully blocks them from locating, communicating with, and providing legal services to their clients and potential clients. For over 16 years, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security has made the location of detained noncitizens available via its Online Detainee Locator System. In September, DHS abruptly changed course and stopped sharing the location of detained people with final orders of removal, either via the locator service or in direct response to queries from family members or attorneys. This policy of mass disappearance has thrown thousands into an administrative black box without any justification. The new policy facilitates the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign by making it more difficult to provide detainees with access to attorneys and the judicial system — and thus more difficult to challenge unlawful detention and pursue lawful pathways to remain in the United States. Noncitizens with final orders of removal may still pursue a number of legal remedies to challenge their detention and deportation — but if they cannot access legal counsel or the courts, they may never have a chance to seek these remedies before they are deported. The lawsuit alleges that ICE’s implementation of this new policy is arbitrary and capricious, and thus a violation of the Administrative Procedure Act. The complaint also alleges that ICE’s policy violates the plaintiffs’ First Amendment rights. Finally, the complaint alleges violations of the Freedom of Information Act because the government failed to publish details of their new policy. The plaintiffs are asking the court to vacate the new policy, and will shortly file a motion to stay the new policy while their case proceeds. The plaintiffs are represented by the National Immigration Law Center, National Immigration Project, the American Civil Liberties Union, the ACLU of Massachusetts, and Annelise Araujo Law. The following are statements from the plaintiffs and their legal counsel: Attorneys representing the plaintiffs: “The Trump administration’s new policy of mass disappearance should send a chill through everybody’s spine. By choosing to hide even the most basic information about thousands of people in its custody, the government is unlawfully blocking their access to legal counsel and the courts, and keeping desperate loved ones in the dark. This shockingly malicious policy was implemented suddenly, without any legal basis or justification, and with immediate, devastating impacts for our clients and the people they serve. The government must reverse course immediately, restore the Online Detainee Locator System, and stop hiding people in its vast network of detention facilities.” Jacquelynne J. Bowman, executive director of Greater Boston Legal Services: “No one should be denied a meaningful opportunity to defend their rights because the government has made it impossible for their lawyer to find them. Even with representation, navigating the legal system is complex for immigrants facing deportation. This arbitrary new administrative change leaves hundreds of thousands of people at risk of potentially life-altering consequences without essential legal help.” Jackie Kelley, director of immigration legal services at the Rian Immigrant Center: “We cannot allow the United States government to indefinitely disappear human beings. If we cannot locate our clients, we cannot pursue the relief for which they are legally eligible. The law gives our clients the right to seek protection. This policy obstructs that right when our clients need it most.” Laura St. John, legal director at the Florence Immigrant & Refugee Rights Project: “The Trump administration is disappearing people within the immigration detention system. This should terrify every single one of us. Thousands of people are no longer being shown on the online detainee locator system, making it impossible for attorneys to locate their clients or identify people who might need emergency legal assistance. How can people in detention possibly have access to due process and safety if there is no way for their families or advocates to know where they are being held?” Aimee Mayer-Salins, deputy program director of legal coordination at the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights: “When someone you love is in ICE custody, they shouldn’t simply disappear into a black hole. Families deserve to know where their loved ones are being held, and this lawsuit is about protecting that basic right.” For more information about Greater Boston Legal Services et al. v. Mullin, visit: https://www.aclu.org/cases/greater-boston-legal-services-et-al-v-mullin


**Court Case:** Greater Boston Legal Services et al. v. Mullin

### New ACLU Film Exposes Human Toll of Immigration Raid in Wilder, Idaho as Families’ Lawsuit Moves Forward


NEW YORK – The American Civil Liberties Union premiered Wilder Raids, an original short film telling the story of two families whose lives were upended by a violent immigration raid at a horse-racing event in Wilder, Idaho, one year ago today. The film follows the families as they reckon with the lasting trauma of the raid and details the ongoing lawsuit brought by the ACLU, ACLU of Idaho, Cooley LLP, and Stoel Rives LLP seeking accountability. One year ago today, more than 200 federal, state, and local law enforcement officers descended on an otherwise peaceful family event at a horse-racing track in Wilder, Idaho. Law enforcement arrived in armored trucks and a helicopter with flashbang grenades and guns drawn and detained approximately 400 spectators – including U.S. citizens and children – for four hours in inhumane conditions before subjecting everyone to suspicionless immigration interrogations. Through interviews with the families and an inside look at the ongoing legal fight, Wilder Raids explores the lasting impact of the raid on those who experienced it and the broader Wilder community. Juana Rodriguez, one of the lead plaintiffs and featured storyteller in the film, is a U.S. citizen who was at the event with her 3-year-old son. After being violently rounded up with hundreds of other families, Rodriguez was placed in zip ties and detained for several hours without food or water. Law enforcement instructed her toddler to hold onto her pocket while Rodriguez remained zip tied and unable to comfort her son. “I was like, why? I have my son with me. I have to take care of him. I was scared. If I overreacted, I felt like they were going to hurt me,” Rodriguez said. “For the longest time, my son begged me for food. He begged me for water … I wish I could have done more in the moment, but I couldn’t. I think that’s what really gets to me till this day.” The families featured in the film filed a lawsuit last February that argues that federal, state, and local law enforcement used criminal warrants as a pretext for a sweeping immigration dragnet at an event where they knew attendees would be predominantly Latino. The complaint further alleges that the agencies conspired to deprive those detained of their Fourth Amendment rights against unreasonable seizures and their right to equal protection regardless of ethnicity. The lawsuit invokes federal civil rights laws enacted after the Civil War to protect people from racialized government violence and provides a potential avenue for holding federal actors accountable for constitutional violations. “Defendants continue to characterize what happened in Wilder as an ordinary warrant execution, but there was nothing routine about the terror they inflicted on hundreds of people trying to spend a Sunday with their families,” said Jenn Rolnick Borchetta, deputy director on policing at the ACLU. “This film makes it impossible to ignore what our clients and their families experienced that day and puts a human face on the reckless violence and cruelty inflicted on the community. One year later, we will not let the government rewrite what happened in Wilder and we will continue fighting to hold those responsible accountable.” “The violent raid in Wilder has had significant ripple effects across many communities in Idaho, which can still be felt today, a year later,” said Leo Morales, executive director of the ACLU of Idaho. “The film reminds us of how critical it is for every American to rise to the challenge of protecting civil liberties. It also highlights how personal and fragile our rights can be if left unprotected from government action. Families cannot simply shake off and ignore the abuse; it is our collective responsibility to seek justice, take action, and make things whole.” The lawsuit is ongoing as the families await a decision on the defendants’ motions to dismiss. On Sept. 8, 2026, plaintiffs filed an opposition brief urging the federal court to allow the lawsuit to proceed. Additional statements from co-counsel are below. Jade Ford, an attorney at Cooley LLP: “This film sends a clear message: the Wilder community will not stand idly by in the face of constitutional violations. Every person in this country is entitled to freedom from unlawful seizure and freedom from discriminatory targeting. Those are not hollow promises—they are vital constitutional guarantees, and the Wilder community intends to see them enforced.” Wendy Olsen, an attorney at Stoel Rives LLP: “All Idaho families should be able to enjoy community and cultural events without fear that their rights will be violated, that their children will be traumatized or that they will be targeted based on their perceived color or national origin. This film bravely tells that story on behalf of the Wilder community.”


**Court Case:** Rodriguez, et al. v. Porter, et al.
